description: Oedipus saves Thebes by solving the riddle of the Sphinx. Yet this victory of the mind opens the door to the most terrible tragedy of all.

hero.hook: A monster asks a riddle. Oedipus answers “Man.” He saves a city and walks straight into his own ruin.

blocks.text: Before he is the tragic hero who kills his father and marries his mother, **Oedipus** is a rescuer. Outside **Thebes**, a city of Boeotia in central Greece, he faces the **Sphinx**, a monster that devours anyone who fails its riddle.

He wins with his mind, not with a sword. But the victory puts him on a throne where he will have to face what he does not know about himself. The myth sets knowledge of humankind against tragic ignorance of oneself.

The Sphinx is a punishment from the gods, often linked to **Hera**. Body of a lion, chest of a woman, wings of a bird, tail of a snake: a hybrid creature. Camped near the city, she cuts the roads. King **Laius** has vanished, killed by a stranger at a crossroads. Thebes has no real ruler.

blocks.caption: The Sphinx of Thebes, keeper of a deadly riddle

blocks.text: Every traveler has to answer. Failure means death. Even the regent [[Creon]] fails. The monster stands for the triumph of the riddle over reason, until a stranger named Oedipus arrives.

sections.title: A monster on the road to Thebes

blocks.text: Oedipus is fleeing Corinth. An oracle has told him he will kill his father and marry his mother. He thinks he is escaping fate. On the road to Thebes, the Sphinx puts its question: what creature has four feet in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening?

blocks.caption: Oedipus before the Sphinx, a victory of intelligence

blocks.text: The word **Sphinx** comes from the Greek *sphingein*, “to squeeze” or “to strangle.” It describes both the way the monster kills and the way a riddle locks up the mind.

Oedipus answers: **“Man.”** As a baby he crawls on four limbs, as an adult he walks on two legs, as an old man he leans on a cane. Beaten, the Sphinx throws itself off the rock. It is a brutal [[plot twist]]. Thebes is free. As promised, Oedipus receives the crown and the hand of the widowed queen, **Jocasta**.

sections.title: “What creature has four feet, then two, then three?”

blocks.text: Oedipus reigns. The city prospers. Years later, a plague strikes. **Apollo** gives the reason: the sickness will stop when the killer of Laius is found. Oedipus opens an investigation with the same energy he once used on the Sphinx.

The irony is cruel. The man who defined “Man” does not know who he is. He has won a public contest of [[dialectics]], a duel of arguments, but he stays blind to his own identity. In **Sophocles**, in *Oedipus the King*, that is the heart of the tragedy.

sections.title: Knowing everything except who you are

blocks.text: The truth breaks out: Oedipus has killed Laius, his father, and married Jocasta, his mother. Jocasta hangs herself. Oedipus puts out his own eyes. Blind, he finally “sees.” He wanders on, leaning on his daughter Antigone, now the three-footed old man of his own riddle.
**Freud** named the [[Oedipus complex]] after this myth, not to turn Oedipus into a monster, but to talk about unconscious desires that civilization teaches us to push down.
The story became a pillar of Western culture: brilliant intelligence, a fate nobody can dodge, and the terrible price of the truth about oneself.
Oedipus frees Thebes by answering “Man” to the riddle of the Sphinx. All that brilliance does not stop him from fulfilling the prophecy without knowing it: the myth of blindness about oneself.

sections.title: The truth and the ruined eyes
